title: Equilibrium Policy Generalization: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Cross-Graph Zero-Shot Generalization in Pursuit-Evasion Games

problems.title: Queue uniqueness does not bound predecessor-query work
problems.source_location: Section 3.2.1, p. 6; Algorithm 1, p. 5; official DP_implementation (2 pursuers).cpp.
claim: The implementation’s runtime argument counts each state being enqueued once but does not retain its predecessor-neighborhood costs.
analysis: On a complete graph with two pursuers and stay actions, all \(n^3\) states are terminal at initialization. Each popped state still inspects \(n\) evader and \(n^2\) pursuer predecessors, yielding order \(n^6\) candidate checks. Unsuccessful scans cost work even when they add no queue entry.
result: The released degree-independent near-linear cost is not established. Bounded-degree behavior or an improved indexed algorithm is not excluded.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: State dependence on agent count and maximum degree, or supply and analyze the promised implicit neighborhood structure including unsuccessful queries.
problems.impact_rationale: This concerns a concrete implementation/runtime justification rather than the central generalization claim.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Equilibrium existence does not imply finite capture everywhere
problems.source_location: Section 3.2.1, p. 6, sentence following complexity paragraph.
claim: The theoretical discussion infers guaranteed finite capture from pure-strategy equilibrium without restricting to a capture-winning region.
analysis: Use three isolated vertices with stay actions, distinct starts for two pursuers and one evader. There is only one possible policy pair, hence a pure equilibrium, but capture never occurs. The model does not impose connectedness or a universally winning region.
result: The finite-capture implication is too broad. A value identity with \(\gamma^{\infty}=0\) can remain valid.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Restrict finite-capture claims to the finite capture-winning region and state the infinite-rank convention separately.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a domain qualification of an auxiliary implication, not a refutation of the whole equilibrium framework.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Imported and new curves use different test distributions
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v2 Section 4.3, PDF p.10, Figure 4; Appendix D.2, differing baseline initial-game filters
claim: Appendix D.2 discloses that the original baseline filtering could not be reproduced and substitutes distance-filtered games for the new evaluation.
analysis: The imported and new Figure 4 curves therefore average different initial-game distributions. Differences in average difficulty can affect scores even without a policy change. The disclosed choice is not hidden leakage, and no ranking reversal is established.
result: The figure juxtaposes protocols; it does not isolate a controlled policy effect.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Evaluate both methods on shared graph edges, starts, exits, horizon and reward/discount conventions, or state the different-protocol scope explicitly.
problems.impact_rationale: The comparison is not controlled at that figure, but the magnitude and direction of its scientific effect are unknown.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: A minimum of sampled returns is not a minimum of expected returns
problems.source_location: Official supplement multi-exit/5vs1-pursuer/test_worker.py run_episode_shortest and stochastic driver.
claim: The stochastic worker minimizes one realized return per exit, whereas worst-case expected utility is \(\min_e\mathbb E[R_e]\).
analysis: In the stated connected five-pursuer, eight-exit example, each exit is captured with probability \(1/8\). Return \(+1\) for capture and \(-1\) otherwise gives worst expected utility \(-3/4\). Independent single draws followed by a minimum instead have expectation \(2(1/8)^8-1\approx-0.99999988\). In general \(\mathbb E[\min_eR_e]\leq\min_e\mathbb E[R_e]\). Deterministic-return evaluation is unaffected.
result: The stochastic release statistic targets a different quantity. No actual published model score is recalculated.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Estimate the conditional mean for each exit using repeated returns, then minimize those estimates and quantify finite-sample selection uncertainty.
problems.impact_rationale: This is an evaluator target mismatch with unmeasured impact on the central benchmark conclusions.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.
